title: Pandas Categoricals, Binning and Method Chaining Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on the pandas category dtype and its memory savings, ordered categories, binning with pd.cut and pd.qcut, and writing readable method-chained pipelines with assign, pipe and query.

chapters.title: Category Dtype: The Mental Model
points: A category column stores a small array of unique values (categories) plus integer codes pointing into it; each row holds only a code
Create with s.astype('category') or pd.Categorical(values, categories=[...]); inspect with s.cat.categories and s.cat.codes
Memory: object strings cost one Python object per row; category costs ~1 to 2 bytes per row plus one copy of each unique value, so low-cardinality columns shrink a lot
Check the saving with df.memory_usage(deep=True); without deep=True object columns are badly under-reported
Best for low cardinality (few unique values, many rows); a near-unique column such as an ID gains nothing and can get larger

layout.note: categories array plus integer codes per row
Interview Point: why is category smaller, when does it not help, how to measure memory

chapters.title: Working with Categories Day to Day
points: Read-only .cat accessor: s.cat.categories, s.cat.codes, s.cat.ordered
Change categories with s.cat.add_categories, remove_categories, rename_categories, remove_unused_categories
Assigning a value not in categories raises an error or gives NaN; add_categories first
Set category dtype at load time: pd.read_csv(path, dtype={'col':'category'}) to avoid a big object column in memory
groupby on a category column includes unobserved categories by default in some versions; pass observed=True to get only values present and run faster

chapters.title: Ordered Categories
points: Ordered category: pd.CategoricalDtype(['low','mid','high'], ordered=True); the order of the list is the order of the values
Without ordering, sort_values sorts by category order, not alphabetical, and comparisons like s > 'low' raise TypeError
With ordered=True you can compare (s >= 'mid'), and use min, max and sort_values in logical order
Convert later with s.cat.as_ordered() or s.cat.reorder_categories([...], ordered=True)
Mistake: leaving plain strings means 'high' sorts before 'low' alphabetically, so sorts and charts come out in the wrong order

layout.note: Interview Point: how to define order, what ordered enables, fix wrong chart order

chapters.title: Binning with pd.cut and pd.qcut
points: pd.cut(x, bins) bins by value: pass an int for equal-width bins or a list of edges for custom bins
pd.qcut(x, q) bins by quantile: each bin holds roughly the same number of rows; q=4 gives quartiles
Intervals are right-closed by default, (0, 10]; use right=False for [0, 10) and include_lowest=True so the minimum value is not dropped to NaN
Use labels=['low','mid','high'] for readable names; the result is a category dtype, ordered=True by default
cut gives unequal counts per bin, qcut gives unequal widths; qcut with many duplicate values raises an error, fix with duplicates='drop'
Values outside the edges of cut become NaN; check with s.value_counts(dropna=False)

chapters.title: Readable Method Chaining Pipelines
points: Method chaining wraps the chain in parentheses and puts one step per line: (df.query(...).assign(...).pipe(fn).sort_values(...))
assign(new=lambda d: ...) adds or replaces columns without mutating the original; the lambda sees the frame as built so far in the chain
query('age > 30 and city == @city') filters with a string expression; use @var for local variables and backticks for column names with spaces
pipe(func, *args, **kwargs) passes the DataFrame into your own function so custom steps stay in the chain; each function should take a frame and return a frame
Mistake: lambda d: vs referencing the outer df, which uses stale data in the middle of a chain; also avoid inplace=True, which returns None and breaks the chain
Keep steps small and named: extract long logic into a pipe function so the chain reads like a recipe, and avoid SettingWithCopy by never assigning into a filtered slice

chapters.title: Categoricals and Pipelines Cheat Sheet
points: Category: s.astype('category'); .cat.categories, .cat.codes, memory_usage(deep=True)
Ordered: pd.CategoricalDtype([...], ordered=True); s.cat.as_ordered(); compare and sort in logical order
cut: by value, edges or int; right=False, include_lowest=True, labels=[...]
qcut: by quantile, equal counts; duplicates='drop' on ties
Chain: (df.query('x > @v').assign(y=lambda d: d.a*2).pipe(clean).sort_values('y')) with no inplace
